title: Optimal Regularization for Performative Learning
claim: Optimal regularization shifts with the strength and sign of the performative effect, and simple approximations locate it accurately.
layout: 3 panels in a row, shared axes style, varying parameter b̄ per panel
description: Three side-by-side line plots share the same format, with regularization strength λ on the x-axis and excess risk on the y-axis. Panels are labeled (a) b̄ = -0.1, (b) b̄ = 0 and (c) b̄ = 0.2. Each panel shows a U-shaped blue dashed theory curve with blue empirical dots and a shaded one-standard-deviation band. An orange dashed first-order approximation curve lies below the blue curve and meets it near the minimum. Vertical lines mark the optimal λ: red for the first-order approximation, violet for the second-order approximation and green for the empirical optimum. The minimum sits at a negative λ in (a), at zero in (b) and at a positive λ in (c). A legend box in each panel overlaps the top of the plot. The eye goes first to the blue parabola-like curves and the clustered vertical lines at their minima.
caption: Excess risk at the performative fixed point $\theta^{\infty}$ in ([ref]), as a function of ridge regularization $\lambda$, for $d = 100$, $\Sigma=I_p$, entries of $b$ uniform in \(\left[\min\{0, 2 \bar b\}, \max\{0, 2 \bar b\} \right]\), $c=0$ and $\sigma = 0.1$. Empirical values (blue dots) are computed from 20 i.i.d.\ trials on $a$ and 5 i.i.d.\ trials on $b$, with error band at 1 standard deviation. Theoretical predictions (blue dashed curves) are from ([ref]) and match perfectly empirical values. First-order approximations (orange dashed curves) are given by $\widetilde{\mathcal R}_{\rm pop}(D, \lambda, \Sigma)$ in ([ref]) and still provide a good match when $\lambda$ is near-optimal. The green vertical line is the optimal regularization obtained by numerically optimizing the excess risk of $\theta^\infty$ ($\lambda^*_{\rm emp}$), the red one is the first-order approximation ($\lambda_{\rm pop}^*$ from ([ref])) and the violet one the second-order approximation ($\lambda^*_{{\rm pop}, 2}$ minimizing ([ref])).
abstract: In performative learning, the data distribution reacts to the deployed model - for example, because strategic users adapt their features to game it - which creates a more complex dynamic than in classical supervised learning. One should thus not only optimize the model for the current data but also take into account that the model might steer the distribution in a new direction, without knowing the exact nature of the potential shift. We explore how regularization can help cope with performative effects by studying its impact in high-dimensional ridge regression. We show that, while performative effects worsen the test risk in the population setting, they can be beneficial in the over-parameterized regime where the number of features exceeds the number of samples. We show that the optimal regularization scales with the overall strength of the performative effect, making it possible to set the regularization in anticipation of this effect. We illustrate this finding through empirical evaluations of the optimal regularization parameter on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
